title: No Names, Only Numbers
subtitle: The workstation is connected, but ordinary websites will not load.

contentReview.reviewNotes: Synthetic DNS-isolation case aligned to current A+ Core 1 troubleshooting, networking, and connectivity objectives. Commands and addresses are fictional documentation examples.

playerRole: Tier 1 service-desk technician for the fictional Northstar Learning Cooperative

allowed: Ask the user focused scope questions
Run read-only network diagnostics on the assigned workstation
Restore the approved automatic DNS configuration on the assigned workstation
Verify service and document the result
requiresEscalation: Modify organization-wide DNS or DHCP services
prohibited: Restart shared routers or switches without authorization
Configure an unapproved public DNS resolver
Claim an organization-wide outage without evidence

learningObjectives: Establish whether a connectivity report affects one user or a broader service
Separate link, gateway, internet reachability, and name-resolution failures
Prefer read-only discriminating tests before configuration changes
Verify both name resolution and browser access after correction

briefing.summary: My laptop says it is connected to Wi-Fi, but websites will not open. I have an online meeting in fifteen minutes. Please restart whatever server is broken.

evidence.label: Original user report
evidence.content: The user reports Wi-Fi shows connected and websites do not open. The user assumes a server is broken; that assumption is not verified.
evidence.coachExplanation: A user report is valuable evidence about symptoms, not proof of scope or cause.

evidence.label: Scope response
evidence.content: Two nearby coworkers are using the same Wi-Fi and can reach the meeting site. Maya's phone also works on the same wireless network.
evidence.coachExplanation: This strongly narrows the problem to the assigned workstation or its user-specific configuration.

evidence.label: IP configuration
evidence.content:
IPv4 Address: 192.0.2.84
Subnet Mask: 255.255.255.0
Default Gateway: 192.0.2.1
DNS Servers: 198.51.100.53
Adapter: Connected
evidence.coachExplanation: The documentation-range addresses are synthetic. The workstation has a plausible local address and gateway, but the DNS value deserves testing rather than immediate judgment.

evidence.label: Gateway reachability
evidence.coachExplanation: The local link and path to the default gateway are working at the time of the test.

evidence.label: Direct IP reachability
evidence.content: The approved connectivity test to 203.0.113.10 succeeds with stable latency.
evidence.coachExplanation: Successful direct-IP access weakens the total-outage and default-gateway hypotheses while keeping DNS or proxy problems plausible.

evidence.label: Name-resolution test
evidence.content: The approved lookup for portal.northstar.example times out while querying 198.51.100.53.
evidence.coachExplanation: This directly tests name resolution and identifies the configured resolver involved in the failure.

evidence.label: Recent change
evidence.content: Maya used a temporary training VPN yesterday. The VPN disconnected unexpectedly before shutdown.
evidence.coachExplanation: This is a plausible change that could explain a stale resolver, but it becomes useful only when combined with the failed resolver test.

evidence.label: Approved configuration restored
evidence.content: The stale VPN-provided DNS value was removed using the approved workstation procedure. The adapter again receives the organization's approved DNS settings automatically.
evidence.coachExplanation: The action is narrow, reversible, authorized, and tied to the evidence.

evidence.label: Service verification
evidence.content: The approved hostname resolves, the meeting site opens, and Maya successfully joins its pre-call device check.
evidence.coachExplanation: Verification covers both the technical symptom and the user's required outcome.

hypotheses.label: The organization's internet connection is down
The laptop has no functioning local network link
The workstation cannot reach its default gateway
A stale VPN-provided DNS resolver remains configured
Only the browser profile is malfunctioning

actions.label: Ask whether coworkers and another device on the same Wi-Fi are affected
actions.immediateFeedback: You established that the report is user-specific rather than organization-wide.
actions.coachHint: Scope questions often eliminate the most expensive hypotheses before any command is run.

actions.label: Inspect the workstation's current IP, gateway, adapter, and DNS configuration
actions.immediateFeedback: You collected the configuration without changing the workstation.
actions.coachHint: Read the actual configuration before assuming that 'connected' means every layer is healthy.

actions.label: Test reachability to the configured default gateway
actions.immediateFeedback: The workstation reaches the local gateway, weakening local-link and gateway-failure explanations.
actions.coachHint: This test isolates the local path without claiming anything yet about DNS or application behavior.

actions.label: Use the approved direct-IP connectivity check
actions.immediateFeedback: Direct-IP reachability works. The total-outage hypothesis is now weak.
actions.coachHint: Compare direct-IP behavior with hostname behavior to isolate name resolution.

actions.label: Run an approved hostname lookup against the configured resolver
actions.immediateFeedback: The configured resolver times out while direct-IP connectivity remains available.
actions.coachHint: This is the most discriminating test once direct-IP reachability has been established.

actions.label: Ask about recent VPN, network, or security-software changes
actions.immediateFeedback: The recent VPN disconnect provides a plausible mechanism for the stale resolver.
actions.coachHint: Recent-change evidence is strongest when it explains an independently observed failure.

actions.label: Restart the shared office router immediately
actions.immediateFeedback: You do not have authorization or evidence for a shared-infrastructure restart. The action would disrupt working users.
actions.coachHint: Do not turn one user's symptom into an office-wide outage.

actions.label: Configure an unapproved public DNS resolver
actions.immediateFeedback: This bypasses approved configuration and may create policy, filtering, or logging problems. It also does not explain the current failure.
actions.coachHint: A workaround is not automatically an authorized correction.

actions.label: Remove and reinstall the wireless adapter driver
actions.immediateFeedback: The action is broad and disruptive, and current evidence does not point to a failed adapter driver.
actions.coachHint: Prefer a test that distinguishes causes before replacing a functioning component.

decision.prompt: Which explanation best fits the evidence you collected?

options.label: A stale VPN-provided DNS resolver remains configured on this workstation
options.feedback: This explanation accounts for working local/direct-IP connectivity, failing hostname resolution, the configured resolver, and the recent VPN change.

options.label: The organization's internet connection is down
options.feedback: Working coworkers, another device, and direct-IP reachability contradict an organization-wide outage.

options.label: The wireless adapter driver has failed
options.feedback: The adapter is connected and reaches both the gateway and an approved public IP.

resolution.prompt: What is the narrowest authorized correction?

options.label: Use the approved workstation procedure to remove the stale VPN DNS value and restore automatic organization-managed DNS
options.feedback: The correction is authorized, narrow, reversible, and tied directly to the observed configuration.

options.label: Change the organization's shared DNS server configuration
options.feedback: The evidence is workstation-specific, and shared infrastructure is outside your authority.

options.label: Close the ticket because the user can join from a phone
options.feedback: A temporary alternative does not resolve or document the workstation fault.

verification.prompt: How do you prove the correction worked?

options.label: Repeat the approved hostname lookup, open the meeting site, and have the user complete its pre-call check
options.feedback: This verifies the failed layer and the user's actual required outcome.

options.label: Confirm only that the Wi-Fi icon still says Connected
options.feedback: The Wi-Fi icon was already connected while the problem existed.

options.label: Restart the laptop and assume a clean startup proves success
options.feedback: A reboot is not proof that name resolution and the meeting workflow now function.

communication.prompt: Build a concise ticket update using the supported statements.

availableMessageParts.text: The issue was limited to one workstation; nearby users and another device remained online.
Direct-IP connectivity worked, but the configured VPN-provided DNS resolver timed out.
I restored the approved automatic DNS configuration on the assigned workstation.
Hostname resolution, the meeting site, and the user's pre-call check all succeeded afterward.
The company DNS server crashed and has been permanently repaired.

debrief.rootCauseExplanation: A temporary VPN left a stale DNS resolver configured on one workstation. Local connectivity, the gateway, and direct-IP access all worked; hostname resolution through the configured resolver failed. Restoring the approved automatic DNS configuration resolved the symptom.
teachingPoints: Connected Wi-Fi proves only part of the path.
Scope before disruption: one affected user should not trigger a shared-infrastructure restart.
Compare direct-IP and hostname behavior to isolate name resolution.
Verification must reproduce the user's required outcome, not merely a status icon.
falseAssuranceWarnings: A successful ping does not prove every application works.
Changing to a public DNS resolver might hide the symptom while violating policy.
A reboot without reproducing the original workflow is not adequate closure.
